Why this research?

account
Why this research?
When someone says “some”, does politeness change what a listener understands, or whether the listener believes it? Earlier work treated answers to a compatibility question as evidence of comprehension. This paper separates comprehension from acceptance of a speaker’s message.

What did the authors predict?
s1
s2
account
What did the authors predict?
Face-threatening messages can trigger a “not all” inference that listeners subsequently reject as untrustworthy. The authors predict additional time at the later question/epistemic-assessment stage, rather than the utterance/comprehension stage. The two studies also examine categorical responses and the effect of clarifying the story.

How the studies connect

account
How the studies connect
Both studies compare face-threat and face-boost versions between participants. Study 1 separates the story, utterance and questions and includes a conversational-implicature question. Study 2 clarifies the speaker’s knowledge and the listener’s purpose, and removes that extra question. The studies are related tests, not two experimental conditions.

What did the paper report?

What is the main takeaway?

account
What is the main takeaway?
The authors argue that understanding an implied message and accepting it as true are distinct processes. They locate the face-threat slowdown in epistemic assessment rather than comprehension. A categorical-only AI trial would test only part of that account; matching its response percentages would not establish the proposed mechanism.

What remains open?
The paper calls for paradigms that more clearly separate comprehension and epistemic assessment. Our replay additionally omits reaction-time analyses and unavailable consent/control/debrief wording. Those replay omissions are not presented as limitations stated by the authors, and the current scholarly pilot is not independently reviewed.
